{{Short description|Subject in mathematics}}
In mathematics, '''measure theory in topological vector spaces''' refers to the extension of [[measure theory]] to [[topological vector spaces]]. Such spaces are often infinite-dimensional, but many results of classical measure theory are formulated for finite-dimensional spaces and cannot be directly transferred. This is already evident in the case of the [[infinite-dimensional Lebesgue measure|Lebesgue measure]], which does not exist in general infinite-dimensional spaces. In fact, there is no nontrivial left-invariant [[Radon measure]] on any Hausdorff, non-locally compact [[topological group]] and infinite-dimensional vector spaces are not locally compact.

The article considers only topological vector spaces, which also possess the [[Hausdorff property]]. Vector spaces without topology are mathematically not that interesting because concepts such as convergence and continuity are not defined there.

== σ-Algebras ==
Let <math>(X,\mathcal{T})</math> be a topological vector space, <math>X^*</math> the [[dual space|algebraic dual space]] and <math>X'</math> the [[Dual space#Topological dual space|topological dual space]]. In topological vector spaces there exist three prominent [[σ-algebra]]s:
* the [[Borel σ-algebra]] <math>\mathcal{B}(X)</math>: is generated by the open sets of <math>\mathcal{T}</math>.
* the [[cylindrical σ-algebra]] <math>\mathcal{E}(X, X')</math>: is generated by the dual space <math>X'</math>.
* the [[Baire set|Baire σ-algebra]] <math>\mathcal{B}_0(X)</math>: is generated by all continuous functions <math>C(X,\mathbb{R})</math>. The Baire σ-algebra is also notated <math>\mathcal{Ba}(X)</math>.

The following relationship holds:
:<math>\mathcal{E}(X,X')\subseteq \mathcal{B}_0(X)\subseteq \mathcal{B}(X)</math>
where <math>\mathcal{E}(X,X')\subseteq \mathcal{B}_0(X)</math> is obvious.

=== Cylindrical σ-algebra ===
{{main|Cylindrical σ-algebra}}

Let <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math> be two vector spaces in duality. A set of the form
:<math>C_{f_1,\dots,f_n,B}:=\{x\in X\colon (\langle x,f_1\rangle,\dots,\langle x,f_n\rangle)\in B\}</math>
for <math>B\in\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n)</math> and <math>f_1,\dots,f_n\in Y</math> is called a [[cylinder set]] and if <math>B</math> is open, then it's an open cylinder set. The set of all cylinders is <math>\mathfrak{A}_{f_1,\dots,f_n}</math> and the set of all open cylinders is <math>\mathfrak{A}^{O}_{f_1,\dots,f_n}</math>. If one takes the product <math>\otimes_{n\in \mathbb{N}} \mathfrak{A}_{f_1,\dots,f_n}</math>, this only produces an [[Field of sets|algebra]]. The σ-algebra
:<math>\mathcal{E}(X,Y)=\sigma\left(\mathcal{Zyl}(X,Y)\right)=\sigma\left(\bigotimes_{n\in \mathbb{N}} \mathfrak{A}_{f_1,\dots,f_n}\right)</math>
is called the cylindrical σ-algebra.<ref name="auto">{{cite book |title=Topological Vector Spaces and Their Applications |first1=Vladimir Igorevich|last1=Bogachev |first2=Oleg Georgievich|last2=Smolyanov|doi=10.1007/978-3-319-57117|lccn=87004931 |series=Springer Monographs in Mathematics| year=2017| publisher=Springer Cham |pages=327–333|doi-broken-date=1 July 2025 }}</ref> The sets of cylinders and the set of open cylinders generate the same cylindrical σ-algebra, i.e. <math>\sigma(\mathfrak{A}_{f_1,\dots,f_n})=\sigma(\mathfrak{A}^{O}_{f_1,\dots,f_n})</math>.

For the [[weak topology]] <math>T_s:=T_s(X,X')</math> the cylindrical σ-algebra <math>\mathcal{E}(X,X')</math> is the Baire σ-algebra of <math>(X,T_s)</math>.<ref name="DF">{{cite book |first=David H. |last=Fremlin |publisher=Torres Fremlin |title=Measure Theory, Volume 4: Topological Measure Spaces |volume=4 |date=2003 |isbn=0-9538129-4-4 |page=479}}</ref> One uses the cylindrical σ-algebra because the Borel σ-algebra can lead to measurability problems in infinite-dimensional space. In connection with integrals of continuous functions it is difficult or even impossible to extend them to arbitrary borel sets.<ref>{{cite book |first=David H. |last=Fremlin |publisher=Torres Fremlin |title=Measure Theory, Volume 4: Topological Measure Spaces |volume=4 |date=2003 |isbn=0-9538129-4-4}}</ref> For non-separable spaces it can happen that the vector addition is no longer measurable to the product algebra of borel σ-algebras because in general <math>\mathcal{B}(X)\otimes \mathcal{B}(Y) \subset \mathcal{B}(X \times Y)</math>, however for the cylindrical σ-algebra one has <math>\mathcal{E}(X,X')\otimes \mathcal{E}(Y,Y') = \mathcal{E}(X\times Y,X'\times Y')</math>.<ref>{{cite book| last1 = Talagrand | first1 = Michel | first2 = Michel |last2 = Ledoux | title = Probability in Banach Spaces: Isoperimetry and Processes | publisher = Springer | year = 1991| isbn = 978-3-642-20211-7| series = Classics in Mathematics | doi = 10.1007/978-3-642-20212-4}}</ref>

===Equality of the σ-algebras===
* Let <math>(X,\mathcal{T})</math> be a topological vector space and let <math>T_s:=T_s(X,X')</math> be the weak topology, then <math>\mathcal{E}(X,X')</math> is exactly the Baire σ-algebra of <math>(X,T_s)</math>.<ref name="DF" />
* Let <math>(X,\mathcal{T})</math> be a separable, metrizable locally convex space and <math>T_s:=T_s(X,X')</math> be the weak topology. Then <math>\mathcal{E}(X,X')</math>, <math>\mathcal{B}_0(X)</math> and <math>\mathcal{B}(X)</math> are equivalent under <math>\mathcal{T}</math> and <math>T_s</math>.<ref name="DF" />

== Measures ==
One way to construct a measure on an infinite-dimensional space is to first define the measure on finite-dimensional spaces and then extend it to infinite-dimensional spaces as a [[projective system]]. This leads to the notion of [[cylindrical measure]], which according to [[Israel Gelfand|Israel Moiseevich Gelfand]] and [[Naum Yakovlevich Vilenkin]], originates from [[Andrei Nikolayevich Kolmogorov]].<ref>{{cite book |first1=Israel Moiseevich |last1=Gelfand |first2=Naum Yakovlevich |last2=Vilenkin |title=Generalized Functionsl, Volume 4: Applications of Harmonic Analysis Vol 4 Applications Of Harmonic Analysis |volume=4 |date=1964 |pages=374}}</ref>

===Cylindrical Measures===
{{Main|Cylindrical measure}}

Let <math>(X, \mathcal{T})</math> be a topological vector space over <math>\mathbb{R}</math> and <math>X^*</math> its [[Dual space#Algebraic dual space|algebraic dual space]]. Furthermore, let <math>F</math> be a vector space of [[Functional (mathematics)#Linear functionals|linear functionals]] on <math>X</math>, that is <math>F \subseteq X^*</math>.

A set function
:<math>\nu: \mathcal{Zyl}(X, F) \to \mathbb{R}+</math>
is called a cylindrical measure if, for every finite subset <math>G := \{f_1, \dots, f_n\} \subseteq F</math> with <math>n \in \mathbb{N}</math>, the restriction
:<math>\nu: \mathcal{E}(X, G) \to \mathbb{R}+</math>
is a σ-additive function, i.e. <math>\nu</math> is a measure.<ref name="auto"/>

Let <math>\Gamma \subset X^*</math>. A cylindrical measure <math>\mu</math> on <math>X</math> is said to have weak order <math>p</math> (or to be of weak type <math>p</math>) if the <math>p</math>-th weak [[Moment (mathematics)|moment]] exists, that is,
:<math>\int_E |\langle f, x \rangle|^p d\mu(f) < \infty</math>
for all <math>f \in \Gamma</math>.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Vakhania |first1=N. N. |last2=Tarieladze |first2=V. I. |last3=Chobanyan |first3=S. A. |title=Probability Distributions on Banach Spaces |publisher=Springer |year=1987 |location=Dordrecht |page=414}}</ref>

=== Radon measure===
{{main|Radon measure}}
Every [[Radon measure]] induces a cylindrical measure but the converse is not true.<ref>{{cite book |first=Laurent |last=Schwartz |title=Radon Measures on Arbitrary Topological Spaces and Cylindrical Measures |series=Notes by K.R. Parthasarathy, Tata Institute of Fundamental Research Lectures on Mathematics and Physics |publisher=Oxford University Press |place=London |date=1973 |pages=172–174 }}</ref> Let <math>E</math> and <math>G</math> be two locally convex space, then an operator <math>T:E\to G</math> is called a <math>(q,p)</math>-radonifying operator, if for a cylindrical measure <math>\mu</math> of order <math>q</math> on <math>E</math> the image measure <math>T_*\mu</math> is a Radon measure of order <math>p</math> on <math>G</math>.<ref>{{cite book |first=Laurent |last=Schwartz |title=Radon Measures on Arbitrary Topological Spaces and Cylindrical Measures |series=Notes by K.R. Parthasarathy, Tata Institute of Fundamental Research Lectures on Mathematics and Physics |publisher=Oxford University Press |place=London |date=1973 |pages=299 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Vakhania |first1=N. N. |last2=Tarieladze |first2=V. I. |last3=Chobanyan |first3=S. A. |title=Probability Distributions on Banach Spaces |publisher=Springer |year=1987 |location=Dordrecht |page=416}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |first=Laurent |last=Schwartz |title=Applications $p$-sommantes et $p$-radonifiantes |journal=Séminaire Maurey-Schwartz (1972–1973) |number=Talk nr. 3 |date= |pages=8 |url=https://www.numdam.org/item/SAF_1972-1973____A3_0/}}</ref>

=== Some results===
There are many results on when a cylindrical measure can be extended to a Radon measure, such as [[Minlos theorem]]<ref>{{cite book |first=Laurent |last=Schwartz |title=Radon Measures on Arbitrary Topological Spaces and Cylindrical Measures |series=Notes by K.R. Parthasarathy, Tata Institute of Fundamental Research Lectures on Mathematics and Physics |publisher=Oxford University Press |place=London |date=1973 |page=233}}</ref> and [[Sazonov theorem]].<ref>{{cite book |first=Laurent |last=Schwartz |title=Radon Measures on Arbitrary Topological Spaces and Cylindrical Measures |series=Notes by K.R. Parthasarathy, Tata Institute of Fundamental Research Lectures on Mathematics and Physics |publisher=Oxford University Press |place=London |date=1973 |page=215}}</ref>

Let <math>A</math> be a [[balanced set|balanced]], [[convex set|convex]], [[bounded set|bounded]] and [[closed set|closed]] subset of a [[locally convex space]] <math>E</math>, then <math>E_A</math> denoted the subspace of <math>E</math> which is generated by <math>A</math>. A balanced, convex, bounded subset <math>A</math> of a locally convex Hausdorff space <math>E</math> is called a Hilbert set if the [[Banach space]] <math>E_A</math> has a [[Hilbert space]] structure, i.e. the norm <math>\|\cdot\|_{E_A}</math> of <math>E_A</math> can be deduced from a [[scalar product]] and <math>E_A</math> is complete.<ref>{{cite book |first=Laurent |last=Schwartz |title=Radon Measures on Arbitrary Topological Spaces and Cylindrical Measures |series=Notes by K.R. Parthasarathy, Tata Institute of Fundamental Research Lectures on Mathematics and Physics |publisher=Oxford University Press |place=London |date=1973 |page=230}}</ref>

==== A theorem by Sazonov-Badrikian  ====
Let <math>E</math> be a [[quasi-complete space|quasi-complete]] locally convex Hausdorff space and <math>E'_c</math> be its dual equipped with the topology of [[uniform convergence]] on [[compact set|compact]] subsets in <math>E</math> . Assume that every subset of <math>E</math> is contained in a balanced, convex, compact Hilbert set. A function of [[Positive definiteness|positive type]] <math>f</math> on <math>E'_c</math> is the [[Fourier transform]] of a Radon measure on <math>E</math> [[if and only if]] the function is continuous for the [[Hilbert–Schmidt operator|Hilbert-Schmidt topology]] associated with the topology of <math>E'_c</math>.<ref>{{cite book |first=Laurent |last=Schwartz |title=Radon Measures on Arbitrary Topological Spaces and Cylindrical Measures |series=Notes by K.R. Parthasarathy, Tata Institute of Fundamental Research Lectures on Mathematics and Physics |publisher=Oxford University Press |place=London |date=1973 |page=239}}</ref>

==== Minlos–Sasonov theorem ====
A slight variant of the theorem is the [[Minlos–Sazonov theorem]] which states that a cylindrical measure is σ-additive and Radon if it's [[Fourier transform]] is continuous in zero in the [[Minlos–Sazonov theorem#Sazonov_topology|Sazonov topology]].
